title: More health data can expand care options without settling who can trust or act on it
source_unit: U.S. Government Accountability Office technology assessment of wearable devices in clinical decision-making
geography: United States health-care technology and clinical settings

denominator.unit: GAO technology assessment of wearable devices with health-related features

potential_use.value: sensors can track vital signs, establish baselines, alert users or clinicians, and provide data for interpretation

potential_benefit.value: could support quicker diagnosis, personalized care plans, and remote monitoring for underserved populations

reliability.value: devices vary in accuracy and reliability

observations.method: GAO review of scientific literature, federal guidance, other documents, stakeholder interviews, agency interviews, and site visits to laboratories, medical and research centers, and manufacturers.
observations.uncertainty: The assessment does not estimate population use, device-specific accuracy, or a causal patient-health effect.
observations.subgroup: Patients, clinicians, caregivers, medical facilities, manufacturers, and underserved populations that may receive remote monitoring.
observations.counterinterpretation: Even imperfect sensors can provide useful supplementary information when clinicians interpret them appropriately; potential benefit is not disproved by variable reliability.

observations.period: 2026; AI-augmented wearable decision-making and clinical integration

denominator.unit: GAO assessment of policy and implementation challenges

integration_problem.value: clinical workflow integration and ensuring patient benefit as intended remain challenges

autonomy.value: the extent to which AI-augmented wearables can make autonomous clinical decisions is unclear

responsibility.value: workflow integration could clarify clinician responsibilities and liability, while requiring resources

certification_tradeoff.value: independent certification could improve information but may create confusion, raise costs, and favor larger manufacturers

observations.method: GAO synthesis of evidence and policy options concerning clinical workflow, data protection, liability, market navigation, and performance certification.
observations.uncertainty: These are policy and implementation considerations, not estimates of actual privacy incidents, liability cases, market concentration, or health outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Patients and clinicians using different devices and facilities with different data systems, resources, and governance practices.
observations.counterinterpretation: Voluntary testing and local workflow improvements may address some barriers without a single national certification or integration model.

boundary: This record measures potential wearable capabilities and reported clinical-integration and governance challenges. It does not establish device use prevalence, patient benefit, privacy harm, health improvement, or inequality magnitude.
